questions.q: In a time of flight mass spectrometer, molecule X is ionised using electrospray ionisation. What is the equation for this ionisation?
questions.explanation: Electrospray ionisation dissolves the sample and adds H+ to form XH+(g). No electrons are removed. The sample starts as a liquid.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of V2+ in the ground state?
questions.explanation: V is [Ar]3d3 4s2. Removing 2 electrons takes both 4s electrons first (4s empties before 3d), leaving 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d3.

questions.q: Which atom has one more proton and two more neutrons than ²³₁₁Na?
questions.explanation: Na has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. One more proton gives 12, two more neutrons gives 14. Mass number = 26, atomic number = 12.

questions.q: Which element has a first ionisation energy lower than that of sulfur?
questions.explanation: Selenium is below sulfur in Group 6. IE decreases down a group due to increased shielding and atomic radius. Cl, O and P are in the same period or above S.

questions.q: Which has the electron configuration of a noble gas?
questions.explanation: Se2- has 36 electrons, same as Kr (a noble gas). H+ has 0, O- has 9, Zn2+ has 28, none of which match a noble gas.

questions.q: Which atom has the smallest number of neutrons?
questions.explanation: 4Li has 3 protons so 1 neutron. 3H has 2 neutrons, 4He has 2, 5He has 3. Li has the fewest.

questions.q: Which is the electron configuration of an atom with only two unpaired electrons?
questions.explanation: 1s2 2s2 2p4 has 2 unpaired electrons in the 2p subshell (Hund's rule: electrons fill singly before pairing). The 2p has 3 orbitals with 4 electrons: paired, single, single.

questions.q: Which shows the electron configuration of an atom of a transition metal?
questions.explanation: A transition metal has a partially filled d subshell. [Ar]4s2 3d8 has a partly filled 3d. 3d0 is not a TM, 3d10 is fully filled, 4p1 is a p-block element.

questions.q: Which atom has the greatest first ionisation energy?
questions.explanation: He has the highest first IE of all elements. It has a full 1s shell, very small radius and no shielding.

questions.explanation: n = cV = 0.01 x 0.01 = 1x10^-4 mol. New concentration = 2x10^-4 mol/dm3. V = n/c = 1x10^-4/2x10^-4 = 0.5 dm3 = 500 cm3. Water added = 500 - 10 = 490 cm3.

options.D: Gold atoms are mainly empty space.

options.B: Gold atoms have electrons in orbitals.

questions.explanation: First IE generally increases across a period. Cl is furthest right in Period 3 (excluding Ar), so has the highest first IE of these four.

questions.explanation: CH3 radical has 9 electrons (6+3). CH4+ also has 10-1=9 electrons. So they have the same number.

questions.q: Which of these atoms has the largest atomic radius?
questions.explanation: Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period. Na is furthest left and lowest in the periodic table of these options.

questions.q: Which of these atoms has the smallest number of neutrons?
questions.explanation: 4Li has 3 protons so 1 neutron. 3H has 2n, 4He has 2n, 5He has 3n. Li has the smallest number.

questions.explanation: He+ to He2+ removes an electron from a 1s orbital with no shielding and high nuclear charge (Z=2). This is the highest energy process listed.

options.B: The ions of both the isotopes contains 26 neutrons

questions.explanation: Calcium sulfate. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols to form esters (acid catalyst). Acyl chlorides are more reactive. Esters have fruity smells and are used as solvents and plasticisers.

questions.q: Which compound can be purified by forming a hot aqueous solution that recrystallises on cooling?
questions.explanation: Benzoic acid. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols to form esters (acid catalyst). Acyl chlorides are more reactive. Esters have fruity smells and are used as solvents and plasticisers.

questions.q: Compound Y has the structural formula CH₃COOCH₂CH(CH₃)₂. Which compound is a position isomer of Y?
questions.explanation: propyl propanoate. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols to form esters (acid catalyst). Acyl chlorides are more reactive. Esters have fruity smells and are used as solvents and plasticisers.

questions.explanation: C 6H 5COOH. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols to form esters (acid catalyst). Acyl chlorides are more reactive. Esters have fruity smells and are used as solvents and plasticisers.

questions.q: Aqueous Cr³⁺ ions are reacted with an excess of aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which product is formed?
questions.explanation: Cr3+ with excess NaOH forms Cr(OH)6 3- because Cr(OH)3 dissolves in excess alkali. It is amphoteric.

questions.q: HA and HB are two strong monobasic acids. 25.0 cm³ of 6.0 mol dm⁻³ HA is mixed with 45.0 cm³ of 3.0 mol dm⁻³ HB. What is the H⁺(aq) concentration, in mol dm⁻³, in the resulting solution?
questions.explanation: Total moles of H+ = (0.025 x 6.0) + (0.045 x 3.0) = 0.15 + 0.135 = 0.285 mol. Total volume = 0.070 dm3. Concentration = 0.285/0.070 = 4.07 mol dm-3.

questions.q: A mixture of N₂ and O₂ gases has a total pressure of 1.42 atm. The mole fraction of N₂ is 0.700. What is the partial pressure, in atm, of O₂ in the mixture?
questions.explanation: Mole fraction of O2 = 1 - 0.700 = 0.300. Partial pressure = mole fraction x total pressure = 0.300 x 1.42 = 0.426 atm.

questions.q: A cell is constructed from two redox systems: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E⦵ = +0.34 V; Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s), E⦵ = +0.80 V. Which statement(s) is/are correct for the cell? (1) The cell potential is 1.14 V. (2) The reaction at the copper electrode is Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. (3) The silver electrode increases in mass.
questions.explanation: EMF = E(more positive) - E(less positive) = +0.80 - (+0.34) = +0.46V. Ag is the positive electrode and Cu is the negative electrode.

questions.q: Which electron configuration(s) is/are correct? (1) Cr atom: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹ (2) Cu atom: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s¹ (3) Fe²⁺ ion: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹
questions.explanation: Moles of Ne = 0.0202/20.2 = 0.001 mol. Each atom loses 1 electron. Electrons = 0.001 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 6.02 x 10^20.

questions.q: A buffer solution is prepared by mixing 200 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, with 600 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium propanoate, CH₃CH₂COONa. Kₐ for CH₃CH₂COOH = 1.32 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. What is the pH of the buffer solution?
questions.explanation: Moles of acid = 0.200 x 2.00 = 0.400. Moles of salt = 0.600 x 1.00 = 0.600. Use Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log(salt/acid).

questions.q: The table shows standard entropies, S⦵ / J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹: CO(g) = 197.6, H₂(g) = 130.6, CH₃OH(l) = 239.7. What is the entropy change, ΔS⦵, in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, for the reaction CO(g) + 2H₂(g) → CH₃OH(l)?
questions.explanation: Delta S = sum of products - sum of reactants. Make sure to multiply by coefficients and check the units are J mol-1 K-1.

questions.q: The redox equilibria for a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell in alkaline solution are: 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq), E⦵ = −0.83 V; ½O₂(g) + H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2OH⁻(aq), E⦵ = +0.40 V. What is the equation for the overall cell reaction?
questions.explanation: In an alkaline fuel cell, the overall EMF = E(cathode) - E(anode). Use the given electrode potentials to calculate.

questions.q: Which enthalpy change(s) is/are endothermic? (1) The bond enthalpy of the C–H bond (2) The second electron affinity of oxygen (3) The standard enthalpy change of formation of magnesium
questions.explanation: Bond enthalpy is always endothermic (breaking bonds needs energy). Second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic because you are adding an electron to an already negative ion.

questions.q: Which statement(s) explain(s) why reaction rates increase as temperature increases? (1) The activation energy is less. (2) Collisions between molecules are more frequent. (3) A greater proportion of molecules have energy greater than the activation energy.
questions.explanation: Temperature increases the kinetic energy of molecules so more collide with energy above Ea. The activation energy itself does not change.

questions.q: 8 3.528 g of a Group 2 metal, M, is reacted with an excess of chlorine. The reaction forms 9.775 g of a chloride. What is metal M?
questions.explanation: Mass of Cl = 9.775 - 3.528 = 6.247g. Moles Cl = 0.176. Trying Ca (Ar=40): 3.528/40 = 0.088. Ratio = 2:1. So CaCl2.

questions.q: Radical reactions are responsible for the catalysed breakdown of the ozone layer. The overall equation is 2O₃ → 3O₂, ΔᵣH = −284 kJ mol⁻¹. The molar gas volume in the ozone layer is approximately 2.5 m³ mol⁻¹. What is the energy released, in kJ, during the breakdown of 1.0 m³ of ozone in the ozone layer?
questions.explanation: The overall reaction is exothermic (negative delta H). The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.

questions.q: A graph of ln k against 1/T (T in K) for a reaction has a gradient with the numerical value of −4420. What is the activation energy, in kJ mol⁻¹, for this reaction?
questions.explanation: Gradient = -Ea/R. So Ea = -gradient x R = 4420 x 8.314 = 36748 J mol-1 = 36.7 kJ mol-1.

questions.q: The equation shows the dissociation of the acid H₃AsO₄ in water: H₃AsO₄ + H₂O ⇌ H₂AsO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺. Which pair is a conjugate acid–base pair?
questions.explanation: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by one H+. H3AsO4 and H2AsO4- are a conjugate pair. H2O and H3O+ are the other pair.

questions.q: What is the number of stereoisomers that Ni(H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂)₂Cl₂ can form?
questions.explanation: The complex has 2 bidentate en ligands and 2 Cl ligands. It can form cis/trans isomers and the cis form has optical isomers. Total = 3.

questions.q: Which property/properties is/are correct for a transition element? (1) The element has atoms with a partially filled d sub-shell. (2) The existence of more than one oxidation state in its compounds. (3) The formation of coloured ions.
questions.explanation: Transition metals have partially filled d subshells and form coloured compounds. Sc and Zn are not true transition metals.

questions.q: Four redox systems relevant to hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells are shown, with E⦵/V values: H₂O(l) + e⁻ ⇌ OH⁻(aq) + ½H₂(g), −0.83; H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ ½H₂(g), 0.00; ½O₂(g) + H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2OH⁻(aq), +0.40; ½O₂(g) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂O(l), +1.23. Which statement(s) is/are correct for an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell? (1) The reaction at the positive electrode is ½O₂(g) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂O(l). (2) The overall cell reaction is H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l). (3) The cell potential is 1.23 V.
questions.explanation: In a fuel cell, the most negative E value is the anode (oxidation) and the most positive is the cathode (reduction). EMF = E(cathode) - E(anode).

questions.q: The equation for the reaction of ICl and H₂ is 2ICl(g) + H₂(g) → 2HCl(g) + I₂(g). The rate constant k for this reaction is 1.63 × 10⁻⁶ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the overall order of the reaction?
questions.explanation: Use the rate equation: rate = k[ICl]^m[H2]^n. Work out the orders from the data given, then find k with correct units.

questions.q: 20 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is added to 10 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. What is the pH of the resulting mixture?
Iodide ions, I⁻(aq), react with MnO₄⁻(aq). The unbalanced equation is I⁻(aq) + MnO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) → IO⁻(aq) + MnO₂(s) + OH⁻(aq). What is the ratio of MnO₂(s) to OH⁻(aq) in the balanced equation?
questions.explanation: Balance using oxidation states. Mn goes from +7 to +4 (gains 3e). I goes from -1 to +1 (loses 2e). Balance electrons transferred.

questions.q: Which statement(s) is/are correct when a catalyst is added to a system in dynamic equilibrium? (1) The rates of the forward and reverse reactions increase by the same amount. (2) The concentrations of the reactants and products do not change. (3) The value of Kc increases.
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally. It does not change the equilibrium position or the value of Kc.

questions.q: Which statement(s) for Group 2 elements is/are correct? (1) The 2nd ionisation energy of magnesium is greater than the 2nd ionisation energy of calcium. (2) A strontium ion, Sr²⁺, contains a total of 6 electrons in s orbitals. (3) The equation for the reaction of barium with water is 2Ba + 2H₂O → 2BaOH + H₂.
questions.explanation: Down Group 2: ionisation energy decreases because atomic radius increases and shielding increases. Reactivity with water increases.

questions.q: Which statement(s) for the complex ion [Co(NH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₃]²⁺ is/are correct? (1) It has cis and trans isomers. (2) It has optical isomers. (3) It is six-fold coordination.
questions.explanation: en (ethane-1,2-diamine) is a bidentate ligand. 3 en ligands give an octahedral complex with 6 coordinate bonds. Check for optical isomers.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, has a concentration of 0.50 mol dm⁻³. pKₐ for CH₃COOH = 4.76 at 25 °C. What is the pH of the ethanoic acid solution at 25 °C?

The feasibility of a chemical reaction depends on the temperature and the signs of ΔH and ΔS. Which row has signs for ΔH and ΔS for a reaction that is feasible at high temperatures but is not feasible at low temperatures?
questions.explanation: A reaction is feasible when delta G is negative. Delta G = delta H - T delta S. Check which combination of signs gives negative G at all temperatures.

questions.q: Two redox systems are shown below: Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Fe(s), E⦵ = −0.44 V; Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E⦵ = +0.34 V. Which species in the two redox systems is the strongest oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: The strongest reducing agent has the most negative E value. Fe has E = -0.44V. Fe is oxidised most easily.

questions.q: Which statement(s) explain(s) the trend in boiling points down the halogens group? (1) The induced dipole–dipole interactions (London forces) become stronger. (2) The covalent bonds become stronger. (3) The permanent dipole–dipole interactions become stronger.
questions.explanation: London forces increase down the group because the atoms have more electrons. More electrons means stronger temporary dipoles.

questions.q: Which statement(s) about a molecule of Cl–N=O is/are correct? (1) It is a polar molecule. (2) It contains 6 lone pairs of electrons. (3) It has a bond angle of 180°.
questions.explanation: ClNO has 1 Cl-N bond and 1 N=O bond. Count lone pairs on each atom. Check if the molecule is polar by looking at its shape.

questions.q: NH₄Fe(SO₄)₂·12H₂O is a hydrated ‘double salt’. A student analyses this double salt using test tube tests. Which row(s) gives/give correct result(s) for the stated test? (1) Reaction with cold NaOH(aq) → green precipitate. (2) Reaction with Ba(NO₃)₂(aq) → white precipitate. (3) Reaction with warm NaOH(aq) → red-brown precipitate and an alkaline gas.
questions.explanation: Fe3+ gives a brown precipitate with NaOH. SO4 2- gives a white precipitate with Ba2+ ions. NH4+ gives ammonia gas when heated with NaOH.

questions.q: For the condensation of ammonia gas, what are the signs of ΔH and ΔS?
questions.explanation: Condensation is exothermic (gas to liquid releases energy) so delta H is negative. Liquid is more ordered than gas so delta S is negative.

questions.q: The equilibrium equation for an indicator, HA, is HA(aq) ⇌ A⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq), where HA is blue and A⁻ is yellow. The indicator is added to a solution and turns yellow. An excess of aqueous sodium hydroxide is then added. Which statement describes how the colour of this solution would be expected to change?

options.A: Colour changes from yellow to blue.
options.B: Colour changes from yellow to green.
options.C: Colour changes from yellow to green and then to blue.

questions.explanation: At low pH, the indicator is in its HA form (blue). At high pH, it is in its A- form (yellow). The colour depends on the ratio of HA to A-.

questions.q: Ammonia and water react to set up an acid–base equilibrium. What are the Brønsted–Lowry acids in the equilibrium mixture?
questions.explanation: In the equilibrium NH3 + H2O = NH4+ + OH-, the acids are the species that donate H+. NH4+ and H2O are the Bronsted-Lowry acids.

questions.q: The three reactions below each form one product only. Which reaction(s) form(s) a product with non-polar molecules? (1) 2CO + O₂ → (2) Si + 2Cl₂ → (3) S + 3F₂ →
questions.explanation: CO2 is a non-polar molecule (linear, dipoles cancel). SiO2 is giant covalent (not molecular). Check each product's structure.

questions.q: Which ion(s) contain(s) one or more unpaired electrons? (1) Mn³⁺ (2) V³⁺ (3) Cu⁺
questions.explanation: Write out the electron configurations. Mn3+ is [Ar]3d4 (4 unpaired). V3+ is [Ar]3d2 (2 unpaired). Cu+ is [Ar]3d10 (0 unpaired).

questions.q: Which compound requires the most energy to convert one mole into its gaseous ions?
questions.explanation: The compound with the highest lattice enthalpy has the smallest ions with the highest charges. MgO has Mg2+ and O2- which are both small and doubly charged.

questions.q: What is the percentage dissociation of a 0.015 mol dm⁻³ solution of methanoic acid, HCOOH (Kₐ = 1.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³)?
questions.explanation: Ka = [H+]^2 / c (for weak acids). [H+] = sqrt(Ka x c). % dissociation = ([H+]/c) x 100.

questions.q: A student adds aqueous potassium carbonate to one test tube and aqueous silver nitrate to a second test tube. The student adds dilute hydrochloric acid to each test tube. Which row has the correct observations?

options.B: K₂CO₃: no change; AgNO₃: no change

questions.explanation: K2CO3 + HCl gives CO2 (effervescence). AgNO3 + HCl gives AgCl (white precipitate).

questions.q: The equations show the electrode potentials of the half-cells used in a lithium-ion cell: Li⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Li, E⦵ = −3.04 V; Li⁺ + CoO₂ + e⁻ ⇌ LiCoO₂, E⦵ = +1.16 V. Which statement is correct in a lithium-ion cell?

options.B: The reaction at the positive electrode is LiCoO₂ → Li⁺ + CoO₂ + e⁻
options.C: The overall cell reaction is Li + CoO₂ → LiCoO₂
options.D: The oxidation number of Co changes from +2 to +1.

questions.explanation: EMF = E(cathode) - E(anode). The more positive half-cell is the cathode. Use the values given.

questions.q: Which substance(s) has/have induced dipole–dipole interactions (London forces) in the solid state? (1) C₂H₆ (2) H₂O (3) Si
questions.explanation: All substances have London forces in the solid state, including ionic and covalent compounds. London forces exist between all molecules and atoms.

questions.q: Which statement(s) is/are correct for the anti-cancer complex Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂? (1) It has bond angles of 90°. (2) The oxidation number of Pt is +4. (3) It forms both optical and cis-trans isomers.
questions.explanation: Pt(NH3)2Cl2 is square planar (90 degree angles). Pt oxidation state: 2x(0) + 2x(-1) + x = 0, so Pt = +2. It has cis and trans isomers.

questions.q: Chlorine trifluoride can be decomposed into its elements forming the equilibrium mixture 2ClF₃(g) ⇌ Cl₂(g) + 3F₂(g), ΔH = +318 kJ mol⁻¹ (ClF₃ colourless gas, Cl₂ green gas, F₂ yellow gas). Which statement(s) is/are correct? (1) The decomposition is a redox reaction. (2) When the equilibrium mixture is cooled, the colour fades. (3) The decomposition has a negative entropy change.
questions.explanation: Use Le Chatelier's principle. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours fewer moles of gas.
Zero order means rate is constant regardless of concentration. The rate-concentration graph is a horizontal line.

questions.q: (b) The rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide shown in Reaction 16.1 can be increased by adding a small amount of powdered manganese(IV) oxide, MnO .
questions.explanation: At equilibrium, concentrations of reactants and products are constant. The graph should show all three concentrations levelling off.

questions.q: Which solution can be added to CH₃COOH(aq) to make a buffer solution?
questions.explanation: A buffer is made from a weak acid and its conjugate base. CH3COONa provides the conjugate base CH3COO- to mix with CH3COOH.

questions.q: A student analyses a solution of a salt. The results are: reaction with NaOH(aq) → green precipitate; reaction with Ba(NO₃)₂(aq) → white precipitate. What is the formula of the salt?
questions.explanation: Green precipitate with NaOH = Fe2+ or Ni2+. White precipitate with Ba(NO3)2 = SO4 2-. Identify the salt from these results.

questions.q: Chlorine has the electron configuration [Ne]3s²3p⁵. Which statement(s) about chlorine is/are correct when it reacts in redox reactions? (1) It can gain one electron to form 1− ions. (2) It can lose its 3s² electrons to form 2+ ions. (3) It can lose its 3p⁵ electrons to form 5+ ions.
questions.explanation: Chlorine can gain an electron (Cl- in ionic compounds), share electrons (Cl2, covalent), or be in positive oxidation states (ClO3-, etc).

questions.q: Which statement(s) about elements in the periodic table is/are correct? (1) The position of an element is determined by its relative atomic mass. (2) The elements in a group have similar chemical properties. (3) Transition elements are used as catalysts in the manufacture of chemicals.
questions.explanation: Elements are arranged by atomic number (not mass). Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.

questions.q: 8 The burette readings from an experiment are shown: Final reading / cm3 29.35 Initial reading / cm3 2.60 The burette has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm3. What is the percentage uncertainty of the titre?
questions.explanation: Titre = 29.35 - 2.60 = 26.75 cm3. Uncertainty = 2 x 0.05 = 0.10 cm3. Percentage = (0.10/26.75) x 100 = 0.37%. Check which answer matches.

questions.q: The overall equation for a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l). The half-equation at the negative electrode is H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻. What is the half-equation at the positive electrode?
questions.explanation: Read the rate from the tangent to the curve at 30 seconds. Rate = change in volume / change in time.

questions.q: Two redox systems are shown below: Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg(s), E⦵ = −2.37 V; Pb²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Pb(s), E⦵ = −0.13 V. Which species is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.explanation: The strongest reducing agent has the most negative E value. Mg (E = -2.37V) is more negative than Pb (E = -0.13V). So Mg is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.q: The rate constant, k, for a first order reaction is 6.19 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. What is the half-life, in s, for the reaction?

A mixture of ethanoic acid and ethanol is left to reach equilibrium. A student determines the amount of ethanoic acid remaining in the equilibrium mixture by titrating the mixture with a solution of sodium hydroxide. Which row of the table shows a suitable indicator (by pH range) for the titration?
questions.explanation: Use the equilibrium expression Kc = [products]/[reactants]. Calculate moles at equilibrium, then concentrations, then Kc.

questions.q: Barium is in Group 2 of the periodic table. Which statement(s) about barium is/are correct? (1) Its outer shell electrons are in an s-orbital. (2) It reacts more vigorously with water than magnesium. (3) It has a higher first ionisation energy than magnesium.
questions.explanation: Barium is in Group 2 so has 2 outer electrons in an s-orbital. It reacts with water. Its hydroxide is soluble.

questions.q: Chromium forms the complex ions [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻. Which statement(s) about the complexes is/are correct? (1) Chromium is in the same oxidation state in each complex ion. (2) The complex ions are different colours. (3) The complex ions have different coordination numbers.
questions.explanation: Both complexes have Cr3+ (oxidation state +3). NH3 and OH- are both neutral/negative ligands. Check coordination number and geometry.

questions.q: Equal amounts of the four compounds are added to the same volume of water. Which compound would produce the most acidic solution?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides and carboxylic acids dissolve in water to produce acidic solutions. The strongest acid produces the most H+ ions.

questions.q: The compound HOOCCH₂CH₂CH₂COOH (pentanedioic acid) is analysed by ¹H NMR spectroscopy. How many peaks are observed in the ¹H NMR spectrum?
questions.explanation: Count the number of different hydrogen environments. Symmetry means some H atoms are equivalent and give the same peak.

questions.q: 0.1 mol of HOOCCH₂COOH are reacted with 0.1 mol of aqueous NaOH. How many molecules of water are formed?
questions.explanation: 0.1 mol of diprotic acid reacts with 0.1 mol NaOH. Only one H+ is neutralised per NaOH. Molecules of water = 0.1 x 6.02 x 10^23.

questions.q: Which reagents could be used to prepare CH₃CH₂CONHCH₃?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides react with amines to form amides. CH3CH2COCl + CH3NH2 gives CH3CH2CONHCH3 + HCl.

questions.q: Ethane reacts with chlorine by radical substitution to form chloroethane. Which radical(s) is/are present in the mechanism? (1) H• (2) Cl• (3) C₂H₅•
questions.explanation: In radical substitution of ethane: initiation gives Cl radicals. Propagation involves CH3CH2 radical and Cl radical. H radical is not formed.

questions.q: Which compound(s) is a/are structural isomer(s) of C₆H₁₂O₂? (1) hexanoic acid (2) ethyl butanoate (3) propyl propanoate
questions.explanation: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements. All three (hexanoic acid, ethyl butanoate, propyl propanoate) are C6H12O2.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with an organic reagent in the presence of a halogen carrier to form phenylethanone (C₆H₅COCH₃). Which organic reagent is required?
questions.explanation: Friedel-Crafts acylation uses an acyl chloride (CH3COCl) with AlCl3 catalyst to add an acyl group to benzene.

questions.q: How many straight-chain structural isomers of C₇H₁₅Cl contain a chiral carbon atom?
questions.explanation: Draw all straight-chain isomers of C7H15Cl. A chiral centre needs 4 different groups. Check each isomer for chirality.

questions.q: 17 The general formula of an α-amino acid is RCH(NH )COOH.
questions.explanation: In mass spec, look at the m/z value and work out which fragment has that mass. Common fragments: CH3 (15), C2H5 (29), CHO (29), OH (17).

questions.q: Which statement(s) support(s) the delocalised model for the structure of benzene? (1) All carbon–carbon bonds have the same length. (2) The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene is less exothermic than expected. (3) Bromine reacts with benzene less readily than with cyclohexene.
questions.explanation: The delocalised model explains: equal bond lengths, enthalpy of hydrogenation being less exothermic than expected for 3 C=C bonds.

questions.q: A solid organic compound can be purified by recrystallisation. Which statement(s) about recrystallisation is/are true? (1) The organic compound is more soluble in hot solvent. (2) The hot solution is cooled before the purified organic compound is collected. (3) The melting point of the purified organic compound is lower than the impure compound.
questions.explanation: In recrystallisation: dissolve in minimum hot solvent, filter to remove insoluble impurities, cool to crystallise, filter to collect crystals.

questions.q: Which of the following could react with C₆H₅CHBrCOOH (2-bromo-2-phenylethanoic acid) to form a carbon–carbon bond? (1) CH₃Cl and AlCl₃ (2) KCN in ethanol (3) CH₃OH and H₂SO₄
questions.explanation: To form a C-C bond: Friedel-Crafts (RCl + AlCl3), or nucleophilic substitution with CN- (KCN in ethanol). Both extend the carbon chain.

questions.q: 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 90 100 m / z Suggest possible structures for the species responsible for peaks Y and Z in the mass spectrum. Y Z [2]
questions.explanation: Count the number of different carbon environments. Symmetry reduces the number of peaks. 4 peaks means 4 unique carbon environments.

questions.q: A student reacts 4.50 g of C₆H₅NH₂ (Mᵣ = 93.0) with excess CH₃COCl in the reaction C₆H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ (Mᵣ = 135.0) + HCl. The reaction produces 3.25 g of C₆H₅NHCOCH₃. What is the percentage yield of C₆H₅NHCOCH₃?
questions.explanation: Moles of C6H5NH2 = 4.50/93.0 = 0.0484. Theoretical yield = 0.0484 x 135.0 = 6.53g. Percentage yield = (actual/theoretical) x 100.

questions.q: 15 The structure of a compound used to treat influenza is shown below. O O O HN NH
questions.explanation: Check chemical shifts against the data sheet. The number and position of peaks tells you which carbon environments are present.

questions.explanation: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. It cannot form tertiary alcohols.

questions.explanation: HCl is a strong monoprotic acid so [H⁺] = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log(0.0500) = 1.30.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid, assuming it is fully dissociated?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ is diprotic, so [H⁺] = 0.200 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log(0.200) = 0.70.

Which expression gives Ka for a weak acid HA?
questions.explanation: Ka is the equilibrium constant for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. For a weak acid alone in water [H⁺] ≈ [A⁻], giving Ka ≈ [H⁺]² / [HA].

questions.q: A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution of a weak acid has pH 2.87. What is Ka?
Which statement explains why the pH of a buffer changes very little when a small amount of acid is added?

options.A: The added H⁺ reacts with the large reservoir of conjugate base
options.B: The buffer neutralises all acids completely
options.C: The added acid is a weak acid
options.D: The water in the buffer dilutes the acid

questions.explanation: A buffer contains a weak acid and a large amount of its conjugate base. Added H⁺ combines with A⁻ to form HA, so [H⁺] barely changes.

questions.q: Which mixture would form an acidic buffer?
questions.explanation: An acidic buffer is a weak acid plus its salt (conjugate base). HCl is strong so cannot buffer, and NH₃/NH₄Cl is a basic buffer.

questions.q: Which Period 3 element reacts most vigorously with cold water?
questions.explanation: Sodium reacts rapidly with cold water, fizzing and forming NaOH and hydrogen. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but vigorously with steam.

questions.q: What is the product when magnesium burns in oxygen?
questions.explanation: Magnesium burns with a bright white flame to form magnesium oxide, MgO, a white solid.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure?
questions.explanation: Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent lattice of Si and O atoms, which gives it a very high melting point. P₄O₁₀ and SO₂ are simple molecular; Na₂O and Al₂O₃ are ionic.

questions.q: Which oxide dissolves in water to give the most alkaline solution?
questions.explanation: Na₂O reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide, a strong alkali (pH about 13 to 14). MgO is only slightly soluble giving pH about 9 to 10, Al₂O₃ is insoluble and SO₂ is acidic.

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of sulfur trioxide with water?
questions.explanation: Sulfur trioxide dissolves in water to form sulfuric acid, a strong acid of about pH 0 to 1.

questions.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide reacts with both acids (forming Al³⁺ salts) and alkalis (forming aluminate ions), so it is amphoteric.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of the solution formed when phosphorus(V) oxide dissolves in water?
questions.explanation: P₄O₁₀ reacts vigorously with water to form phosphoric(V) acid, H₃PO₄, a fairly strong acid giving a pH of about 0 to 1 in concentrated solution.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation: MgO is ionic with small, doubly charged ions giving a very strong lattice (melting point about 2850 °C), higher than SiO₂ (about 1610 °C). SO₂ is a gas at room temperature.

questions.q: Why does MgO have a higher melting point than Na₂O?

options.B: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and smaller radius than Na⁺, so the ionic attraction is stronger
options.C: MgO has a simple molecular structure
options.D: Na₂O has more ions per formula unit

questions.explanation: Both are ionic lattices. The greater charge and smaller size of Mg²⁺ gives a stronger electrostatic attraction to the oxide ions.

questions.q: Why is sulfur dioxide a gas at room temperature while silicon dioxide is a solid with a high melting point?

options.A: SO₂ is ionic and SiO₂ is covalent
options.B: SO₂ is simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces; SiO₂ is a giant covalent lattice

questions.explanation: Only weak van der Waals forces and dipole–dipole forces act between SO₂ molecules. Melting SiO₂ requires breaking many strong covalent bonds.

questions.q: Which ionic equation shows the reaction of sodium oxide with water?
questions.explanation: The oxide ion is a strong base and removes a proton from water: O²⁻ + H₂O → 2OH⁻. Overall Na₂O + H₂O → 2Na⁺ + 2OH⁻.

questions.q: Which equation shows aluminium oxide behaving as a base?
questions.explanation: Reacting with an acid to give a salt and water is basic behaviour. The reaction with NaOH shows acidic behaviour.

questions.q: Which equation shows silicon dioxide behaving as an acid?
questions.explanation: SiO₂ is insoluble in water but reacts with hot concentrated alkali to form a silicate, which is acidic behaviour.

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of sulfur with oxygen?
questions.explanation: Sulfur burns in oxygen with a blue flame to form sulfur dioxide. SO₃ is made industrially from SO₂ using a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.

questions.q: Which Period 3 element has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation: Silicon has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds throughout, giving a melting point of about 1410 °C.

questions.q: Phosphorus burns in oxygen to form phosphorus(V) oxide. Which is the correct formula?
questions.explanation: Phosphorus burns with a white flame to form phosphorus(V) oxide, P₄O₁₀, a white solid.

questions.q: What is observed when magnesium reacts with steam?

options.A: A slow reaction with a few bubbles
options.B: A bright white flame and a white solid
options.C: A violet flame and a colourless gas

questions.explanation: Heated magnesium reacts vigorously with steam, burning with a bright white flame to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of a solution formed when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water?
questions.explanation: SO₂ forms sulfurous acid, H₂SO₃, a weak acid with pH around 2 to 3.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide has the lowest melting point?
questions.explanation: SO₃ is simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces and melts at about 17 °C. P₄O₁₀ is also molecular but larger, with stronger van der Waals forces.

questions.q: Which statement describes the trend in the oxides from Na₂O to SO₃?

options.A: Ionic to covalent, basic to acidic
options.B: Covalent to ionic, acidic to basic

questions.explanation: Bonding changes from ionic (Na₂O, MgO) through ionic with covalent character (Al₂O₃) to covalent (SiO₂ to SO₃). Character changes from basic to amphoteric to acidic.

questions.q: The equation Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂ represents which reaction?
questions.explanation: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water to form magnesium hydroxide. With steam it forms MgO instead.

questions.q: Why is phosphorus(V) oxide acidic while magnesium oxide is basic?

options.A: P₄O₁₀ is ionic and MgO is covalent
options.B: P₄O₁₀ is covalent and reacts with water to donate protons; MgO contains O²⁻ ions which accept protons

questions.explanation: Covalent non-metal oxides form acids with water. The oxide ion in ionic metal oxides acts as a base, forming OH⁻ in water or reacting directly with acids.

questions.q: Which pair of oxides would react together?
questions.explanation: A basic oxide and an acidic oxide react to form a salt: MgO + SO₃ → MgSO₄. Two basic or two acidic oxides do not react with each other.

questions.q: Which ion has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁵?
questions.explanation: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Removing the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron leaves [Ar] 3d⁵. Mn³⁺ is 3d⁴, Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ and Cr²⁺ is 3d⁴.

questions.q: Why is zinc not classed as a transition metal?

options.B: Its only common ion, Zn²⁺, has a full 3d subshell
options.D: It is not in the d block

questions.explanation: A transition metal forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell. Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so zinc compounds are white and zinc shows only one oxidation state.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of the complex [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
questions.explanation: Coordination number is the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion. Each water molecule forms one coordinate bond, so it is 6.

questions.q: Which shape does [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ have?
questions.explanation: Two ligands around a central ion give a linear complex, as in Tollens' reagent.

questions.q: Which complex is used as Tollens' reagent to test for aldehydes?
questions.explanation: Tollens' reagent contains the linear diamminesilver(I) ion. Aldehydes reduce Ag⁺ to silver, forming the silver mirror.

questions.q: What is the colour of a solution containing [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ ions?
questions.explanation: Hexaaquairon(II) is pale green. Iron(III) solutions appear yellow or brown because of partial hydrolysis.

questions.q: Why is a solution of [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ more acidic than a solution of [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺?

options.A: Fe³⁺ has a lower charge density
options.B: Fe³⁺ has a higher charge density so it polarises the O–H bonds in the water ligands more, releasing H⁺

questions.explanation: The smaller, more highly charged Fe³⁺ pulls electron density from the coordinated water, weakening the O–H bonds so protons are more easily lost (hydrolysis).

questions.q: Which equation shows the hydrolysis of the hexaaquaaluminium ion?
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis is the loss of a proton from a coordinated water molecule to a solvent water molecule, producing H₃O⁺ and making the solution acidic.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium hydroxide solution is added dropwise to a solution of copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ forms a pale blue precipitate of Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂, which is insoluble in excess NaOH.

questions.q: Which hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric and dissolves in excess OH⁻ to form the colourless aluminate ion [Al(OH)₄]⁻. The copper and iron hydroxides do not dissolve.

questions.q: What is observed when iron(II) hydroxide precipitate is left standing in air?

options.A: It turns from green to brown as Fe(II) is oxidised to Fe(III)

questions.explanation: Green Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂ is oxidised by oxygen in the air to brown Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃.

questions.q: Which precipitate forms when excess ammonia is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.B: A blue precipitate that dissolves to give a deep blue solution

questions.explanation: Ammonia first acts as a base, giving blue Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂. Excess ammonia then acts as a ligand, forming deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.

questions.q: What is the formula of the complex formed when excess concentrated ammonia is added to a copper(II) solution?
questions.explanation: Only four of the six water ligands are replaced, giving the deep blue tetraamminediaquacopper(II) ion.

questions.q: Which observation is made when sodium carbonate solution is added to a solution of iron(III) chloride?

options.B: A brown precipitate and bubbles of carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Hexaaqua 3+ ions are acidic enough to react with carbonate ions to release CO₂, and the brown hydroxide precipitates. 2+ ions form the metal carbonate instead, with no gas.

questions.q: Which product forms when sodium carbonate is added to a solution containing [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
questions.explanation: M²⁺ ions are not acidic enough to liberate CO₂, so a blue-green precipitate of the carbonate, CuCO₃, forms.

questions.q: Which equation shows aluminium hydroxide dissolving in excess sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: The amphoteric hydroxide loses a further proton to OH⁻ to form the colourless aluminate ion [Al(H₂O)₂(OH)₄]⁻ (often written [Al(OH)₄]⁻).

questions.q: Which equation shows aluminium hydroxide dissolving in excess hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Acid protonates the OH⁻ ligands back to water, regenerating the hexaaqua ion. This is the acidic side of amphoteric behaviour.

questions.q: What is observed when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.A: The solution turns from blue to yellow-green

questions.explanation: Chloride ions replace the water ligands to form the yellow [CuCl₄]²⁻ ion. The mixture of blue and yellow often appears green.

questions.q: Why does the coordination number fall from 6 to 4 when water ligands are replaced by chloride ions?

options.B: Chloride ions are larger than water molecules, so fewer can fit around the metal ion

questions.explanation: The larger Cl⁻ ligands cannot pack six around the central ion, so a tetrahedral four-coordinate complex forms.

questions.q: What is the shape of [CuCl₄]²⁻?
questions.explanation: Four large chloride ligands arrange tetrahedrally around the copper(II) ion.

questions.q: Which observation is made when ammonia solution is added dropwise and then in excess to iron(III) chloride solution?
questions.explanation: Ammonia acts as a base, forming brown Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃. Iron(III) does not form an ammine complex under these conditions so the precipitate does not dissolve.

questions.q: Which ion gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess?
questions.explanation: Aluminium hydroxide is white and amphoteric, dissolving in excess alkali. The other three hydroxides are coloured and do not dissolve.

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ with two hydroxide ions?
questions.explanation: Each hydroxide ion removes a proton from a coordinated water molecule. The neutral hydroxide complex precipitates, releasing two water molecules.

questions.q: Which solution has the lowest pH?
questions.explanation: 3+ hexaaqua ions hydrolyse much more than 2+ ions because of their higher charge density, so [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺ gives the most acidic solution (pH about 3).

questions.q: What is the colour of the [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ion itself?
questions.explanation: The hexaaquairon(III) ion is pale violet, but solutions appear yellow-brown because of hydrolysis to [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺.

questions.q: Which test distinguishes between solutions of iron(II) and iron(III) ions?

options.A: Adding sodium hydroxide: green precipitate for Fe(II), brown for Fe(III)

questions.explanation: Iron(II) gives green Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂ and iron(III) gives brown Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃. Ammonia solution gives the same result.

questions.q: What is the name of the reaction in which water ligands around a metal ion are replaced by ammonia molecules?
questions.explanation: Ligand substitution is the exchange of one ligand for another. Acid–base hydrolysis (deprotonation) is a different type of reaction.

questions.q: Which compound shows optical isomerism?
questions.explanation: Optical isomers need a chiral carbon with four different groups. In butan-2-ol, C2 is bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃.

questions.q: How many chiral centres are there in 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid), CH₃CH(OH)COOH?
questions.explanation: The central carbon carries H, OH, CH₃ and COOH, four different groups, so there is one chiral centre.

questions.q: What is a racemic mixture?

options.A: A mixture of two different compounds
options.B: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers
options.C: A mixture of a ketone and an aldehyde
options.D: A mixture that rotates plane-polarised light clockwise

questions.explanation: A racemate contains equal amounts of the two optical isomers, so their rotations of plane-polarised light cancel and the mixture is optically inactive.

questions.q: Why does the nucleophilic addition of HCN to butanone produce a racemic mixture?

options.A: The product has no chiral centre
options.B: The CN⁻ ion can attack the planar carbonyl group from either side with equal probability
options.D: Butanone is itself a racemic mixture

questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon is planar (sp²), so attack from above or below is equally likely, giving equal amounts of each enantiomer.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to reduce propanone to propan-2-ol?
questions.explanation: Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) provides the hydride ion nucleophile that reduces carbonyl compounds to alcohols. Ketones give secondary alcohols.

questions.q: What is the nucleophile in the reduction of an aldehyde by NaBH₄?
questions.explanation: The hydride ion H⁻ from NaBH₄ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon in the first step of nucleophilic addition.

questions.q: What type of reaction occurs when propanal reacts with HCN?
questions.explanation: The C=O bond is polar; the CN⁻ nucleophile adds to the δ+ carbon and the oxygen gains a proton, forming a hydroxynitrile.

questions.q: What is the product of the reaction between ethanal and HCN (KCN followed by acid)?
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon gains CN and OH, giving CH₃CH(OH)CN, 2-hydroxypropanenitrile. The carbon chain is lengthened by one.

questions.q: Which hazard is associated with using KCN in the hydroxynitrile synthesis?

options.B: It is a powerful oxidising agent
options.C: It can release toxic HCN gas

questions.explanation: Cyanide salts react with acid to give hydrogen cyanide, a highly toxic gas, so the reaction is carried out in a fume cupboard.

questions.q: Which observation is made when Fehling's solution is warmed with propanal?
questions.explanation: Aldehydes reduce the blue Cu²⁺ complex in Fehling's solution to a brick red precipitate of copper(I) oxide. Ketones give no change.

questions.q: Which compound gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
questions.explanation: Only aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens' reagent, reducing Ag⁺ to metallic silver.

questions.q: Which is the correct IUPAC name for CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The C=O is on the second carbon of a four-carbon chain and is a ketone, so butan-2-one (butanone).

questions.q: Which compound is produced when butanone is reduced?
questions.explanation: Reducing a ketone with NaBH₄ gives a secondary alcohol with the OH on the same carbon as the original C=O.

questions.q: Which statement about enantiomers is correct?

options.B: They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions by equal amounts
options.D: They are also called structural isomers

questions.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except for the direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light. They are stereoisomers, not structural isomers.

questions.q: Which molecule is NOT chiral?
questions.explanation: Propan-2-ol has two identical CH₃ groups on the carbon bearing the OH, so there are not four different groups and it is not chiral.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to make an ester from a carboxylic acid?

options.A: An alcohol and concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst

questions.explanation: Esterification is a reversible reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, catalysed by a strong acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄, heated under reflux.

questions.q: What is the name of the ester formed from ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: The alkyl group comes from the alcohol (propyl) and the -oate from the acid (ethanoate).

questions.q: Which products form when methyl propanoate is hydrolysed with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Alkaline hydrolysis gives the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid. The ester is methyl propanoate so the alcohol part is methanol.

questions.q: What is produced when a vegetable oil is heated with sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: Saponification: the triglyceride ester is hydrolysed to the sodium salts of fatty acids (soap) and propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol).

questions.q: Biodiesel is made by reacting vegetable oils with

options.B: methanol in the presence of a catalyst

questions.explanation: Transesterification of the triglyceride with methanol (KOH catalyst) gives methyl esters of fatty acids (biodiesel) and glycerol.

questions.q: Which reagent reacts with ethanoyl chloride to form ethanamide?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides react with ammonia to form primary amides: CH₃COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl.

questions.q: Which product forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine?
questions.explanation: Primary amines react with acyl chlorides to give N-substituted amides: CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ + HCl.

questions.q: What is the by-product when ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides undergo nucleophilic addition–elimination with alcohols, forming an ester and HCl. Unlike esterification with a carboxylic acid the reaction is rapid and not reversible.

questions.q: Which observation is made when ethanoyl chloride is added to water?

options.B: A vigorous reaction with steamy fumes of HCl

questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides hydrolyse violently in water to form the carboxylic acid and hydrogen chloride, seen as white steamy fumes.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of using ethanoic anhydride rather than ethanoyl chloride to make aspirin?

options.B: It is cheaper, less corrosive and does not produce HCl
options.D: It is a gas so is easier to handle

questions.explanation: Ethanoic anhydride is cheaper, safer to handle, less vulnerable to hydrolysis and the by-product is ethanoic acid rather than corrosive HCl.

questions.q: What type of mechanism do acyl chlorides undergo with nucleophiles?
questions.explanation: The nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon, then the C=O re-forms as Cl⁻ is eliminated, followed by loss of H⁺.

questions.q: Which compound is a weak acid that reacts with sodium carbonate to release carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are weak acids but are acidic enough to liberate CO₂ from carbonates and hydrogencarbonates, a test that distinguishes them from phenols and alcohols.

questions.q: Which is a common use of esters?
questions.explanation: Esters have pleasant smells (flavourings and perfumes), are good solvents, and are added to polymers as plasticisers to make them more flexible.

questions.q: The reaction of ethanoic anhydride with ethanol produces
questions.explanation: (CH₃CO)₂O + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + CH₃COOH. One acyl group forms the ester and the other leaves as ethanoic acid.

questions.q: Which statement about the bonding in benzene is correct?

options.A: It has three C=C double bonds
options.B: Each carbon donates one electron to a delocalised π system above and below the ring
options.C: All the carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
options.D: The C–C bonds alternate between short and long

questions.explanation: Each carbon uses three electrons in σ bonds and the fourth p electron overlaps sideways to form a delocalised ring. All six C–C bonds are the same length, between a single and a double bond.

questions.q: Which piece of evidence does NOT support the delocalised model of benzene?

options.A: All C–C bond lengths are equal
options.B: Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition
options.C: The enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than expected for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene
options.D: Benzene has the molecular formula C₆H₆

questions.explanation: The molecular formula alone does not distinguish between the Kekulé and delocalised models. The other three observations all show that benzene is more stable than a triene and has no separate double bonds.

questions.q: What is the shape of the benzene molecule?
questions.explanation: Benzene is planar; each carbon is trigonal planar (sp²) with bond angles of 120°.

questions.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic substitution rather than electrophilic addition?

options.A: Addition would break the stable delocalised ring
options.B: Benzene has no electrons to donate
options.D: Substitution is faster for all hydrocarbons

questions.explanation: Addition would destroy the delocalised π system and lose its stabilisation (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹). Substitution keeps the ring intact.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to nitrate benzene?

options.B: Concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at about 50 °C

questions.explanation: Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates HNO₃ to generate the NO₂⁺ electrophile. Keeping the temperature around 50 °C prevents further nitration.

questions.q: Which species is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
questions.explanation: The nitronium ion NO₂⁺ is formed from HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.

questions.q: Which equation shows the formation of the nitronium ion?
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to form NO₂⁺. The sulfuric acid is regenerated at the end so it acts as a catalyst.

questions.q: What is the role of sulfuric acid in the nitration of benzene?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ is used to generate NO₂⁺ and is re-formed when H⁺ is lost from the intermediate, so it is a catalyst.

questions.q: Why is the nitration of benzene an important industrial reaction?

options.A: Nitrobenzene is used as a fuel
options.B: Nitro compounds are reduced to aromatic amines used to make dyes and pharmaceuticals

questions.explanation: Nitroarenes are reduced (Sn/HCl) to arylamines such as phenylamine, which are starting materials for dyes, and polynitro compounds are explosives.

questions.q: Which catalyst is used in the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene?
questions.explanation: Aluminium chloride accepts a chloride ion from the acyl chloride to generate the acylium ion electrophile, RCO⁺.

questions.q: What is the electrophile in the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: CH₃COCl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CO⁺ + AlCl₄⁻. The acylium ion then attacks the benzene ring.

questions.q: What is the product of the reaction between benzene and ethanoyl chloride with AlCl₃?
questions.explanation: Acylation attaches a COCH₃ group to the ring, giving the ketone phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃.

questions.q: Which conditions are used for Friedel–Crafts acylation?

options.B: Heat under reflux with anhydrous AlCl₃ in a dry non-aqueous solvent

questions.explanation: AlCl₃ reacts with water, so the reaction must be anhydrous. Reflux is used to drive the reaction.

questions.q: In the mechanism of electrophilic substitution, what happens in the final step?

options.B: A proton is lost from the intermediate, restoring the delocalised ring

questions.explanation: The positively charged intermediate (with a partially delocalised ring) loses H⁺ to regenerate the full aromatic system.

questions.q: Why is the enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene (−208 kJ mol⁻¹) less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene (−360 kJ mol⁻¹)?

options.B: The delocalised electrons make benzene about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than a hypothetical triene

questions.explanation: The difference of about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ is the delocalisation (resonance) energy, showing benzene is more stable than if it contained three isolated C=C bonds.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of methylbenzene?
questions.explanation: Methylbenzene (toluene) is a benzene ring with one hydrogen replaced by CH₃: C₆H₅CH₃, or C₇H₈.

questions.q: What type of reaction is the conversion of nitrobenzene to phenylamine?
questions.explanation: The NO₂ group is reduced to NH₂ using tin and concentrated HCl (or H₂ with a nickel catalyst), followed by NaOH to liberate the free amine.

questions.q: Why is the nitration of benzene kept below about 55 °C?

options.B: To prevent further nitration giving dinitrobenzene
options.C: To stop the sulfuric acid decomposing

questions.explanation: At higher temperatures a second NO₂ group can be substituted, giving 1,3-dinitrobenzene as an impurity.

questions.q: Which bond angle is found in benzene?
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom is trigonal planar with three σ bonds, so the bond angles are 120°.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares cyclohexene and benzene with bromine water?

options.B: Cyclohexene decolourises bromine water; benzene does not
options.C: Benzene decolourises bromine water; cyclohexene does not

questions.explanation: Cyclohexene has a localised C=C with high electron density that attracts Br₂ (electrophilic addition). Benzene's delocalised electrons are spread out and not polarising enough to react without a catalyst.

questions.q: How many σ and π electrons are in the delocalised system of benzene?
questions.explanation: Each of the six carbons contributes one p electron, giving a delocalised system of six π electrons above and below the plane of the ring.

questions.q: Which intermediate forms during the nitration of benzene?

options.C: A positively charged intermediate with a partially delocalised ring (arenium ion)

questions.explanation: The NO₂⁺ electrophile accepts a pair of electrons from the ring, forming a cationic intermediate in which delocalisation is interrupted at one carbon.

questions.q: Which of these nitrogen compounds is the strongest base?
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen (positive inductive effect), making the lone pair more available to accept a proton. In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the ring; amides are not basic.

questions.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia?

options.A: It has no lone pair on the nitrogen
options.B: The nitrogen lone pair is partially delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton
options.C: The benzene ring donates electrons to nitrogen

questions.explanation: Delocalisation of the lone pair into the aromatic π system reduces the electron density on the nitrogen.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to prepare ethylamine from bromoethane?

options.A: Excess ammonia in ethanol, heated under pressure

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution with excess concentrated ammonia in a sealed tube gives the primary amine. Excess ammonia reduces further substitution to secondary and tertiary amines.

questions.q: Why is excess ammonia used when making a primary amine from a halogenoalkane?

options.B: To reduce further substitution of the amine product

questions.explanation: The amine formed is itself a nucleophile and can react with more halogenoalkane. Excess ammonia makes it more likely that the halogenoalkane collides with NH₃.

questions.q: Which method gives the purer product when making a primary amine, and why?

options.A: Reduction of a nitrile, because no further substitution can occur
options.B: Reaction of a halogenoalkane with ammonia, because the reaction is faster
options.C: Reduction of a nitrile, because it uses no catalyst
options.D: Reaction with ammonia, because ammonia is cheap

questions.explanation: Reducing a nitrile (with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni) gives only the primary amine. The ammonia route gives a mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces propanenitrile to propylamine?
questions.explanation: Lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) (or H₂ with a nickel catalyst) reduces the C≡N group to CH₂NH₂.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to reduce nitrobenzene to phenylamine?

options.A: Tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, then sodium hydroxide

questions.explanation: Sn/conc. HCl reduces NO₂ to the phenylammonium ion; NaOH is then added to liberate the free phenylamine.

questions.q: Which product forms when excess bromoethane reacts with ammonia?

options.B: A quaternary ammonium salt, tetraethylammonium bromide

questions.explanation: With excess halogenoalkane, substitution continues through secondary and tertiary amines to the quaternary ammonium salt (C₂H₅)₄N⁺Br⁻.

questions.q: Quaternary ammonium salts with long hydrocarbon chains are used as

options.B: cationic surfactants in fabric softeners and hair conditioners

questions.explanation: The positively charged head is attracted to negatively charged surfaces such as fibres and hair, reducing static and softening.

questions.q: What is the product when ethylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Amines are bases and accept a proton: CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

questions.q: What type of reaction occurs between ethylamine and ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: The amine nitrogen acts as a nucleophile towards the acyl chloride, forming an N-substituted amide and HCl.

questions.q: In which reaction does the amine act as a nucleophile rather than a base?
questions.explanation: With a halogenoalkane the lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon (nucleophilic substitution). With acids the lone pair accepts a proton (base).

questions.q: Which is a secondary amine?
questions.explanation: A secondary amine has two alkyl groups on the nitrogen. One is primary, three is tertiary and four is a quaternary ammonium ion.

questions.q: Which is a tertiary amine?
questions.explanation: Trimethylamine has three carbon groups attached to nitrogen.

questions.q: Why are amines soluble in water?

options.B: They form hydrogen bonds with water through the N–H group and the lone pair
options.D: They react with water to form hydrogen gas

questions.explanation: The N–H bonds and the lone pair on nitrogen allow hydrogen bonding with water. Solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens.

questions.q: Which compound is produced when phenylamine reacts with excess bromoethane?

options.B: A mixture including N,N-diethylphenylamine and a quaternary salt

questions.explanation: The nitrogen keeps reacting with the halogenoalkane while it has a lone pair, giving successive substitution products.

questions.q: Why does the base strength increase from ammonia to methylamine to dimethylamine?

options.A: The number of lone pairs increases
options.B: Each alkyl group pushes more electron density onto nitrogen, making the lone pair more available

questions.explanation: The positive inductive effect of alkyl groups increases the electron density on the nitrogen lone pair, increasing its ability to accept a proton.

questions.q: The mechanism for the reaction between ammonia and bromoethane is
questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon and the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, releasing Br⁻. A second ammonia then removes H⁺.

questions.q: Which compound would be formed by reducing CH₃CH₂CN?
questions.explanation: Reduction of the nitrile converts C≡N to CH₂NH₂, so propanenitrile gives propylamine, which keeps all three carbons.

questions.q: Which type of polymerisation forms Terylene (PET)?

options.B: Condensation polymerisation of a diol and a dicarboxylic acid
options.C: Condensation polymerisation of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid

questions.explanation: Terylene is a polyester made from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and ethane-1,2-diol. Each ester link forms with the loss of a water molecule.

questions.q: Which pair of monomers forms nylon-6,6?
questions.explanation: Nylon-6,6 is a polyamide: the diamine and dicarboxylic acid each have six carbons and link through amide (peptide) bonds.

questions.q: What small molecule is lost when a polyamide forms from a diamine and a dioyl dichloride?
questions.explanation: With an acyl chloride, each amide link forms with the elimination of HCl. With a dicarboxylic acid, water is lost instead.

questions.q: Why are polyalkenes such as poly(ethene) not biodegradable?

options.B: The C–C and C–H bonds are non-polar and unreactive, so enzymes and water cannot attack them

questions.explanation: Polyalkenes are saturated hydrocarbons. There is no polar bond for a nucleophile or enzyme to attack, so they persist in landfill.

questions.q: Why can polyesters and polyamides be hydrolysed?

options.A: They contain polar ester or amide links that can be attacked by water, acid or alkali

questions.explanation: The C=O carbon in an ester or amide link is δ+ and can be attacked by nucleophiles such as water or OH⁻, breaking the chain. This makes them biodegradable.

questions.q: Which intermolecular force acts between nylon chains and gives nylon its strength?

options.B: Hydrogen bonding between N–H and C=O groups

questions.explanation: The N–H of one amide link forms a hydrogen bond to the C=O of an adjacent chain, holding the chains strongly together.

questions.q: Which intermolecular forces act between poly(propene) chains?
questions.explanation: Poly(propene) is a non-polar hydrocarbon, so only van der Waals (induced dipole) forces hold the chains together.

questions.q: What is the repeating unit of the polymer formed from HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH and HO–CH₂CH₂–OH?
questions.explanation: An ester link forms between each COOH and OH. The repeating unit contains one unit of each monomer joined by two ester links.

questions.q: Kevlar is a polyamide made from benzene-1,4-diamine and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Why is it so strong?

options.B: The rigid aromatic rings and hydrogen bonds between chains hold the straight chains in highly ordered sheets
options.D: The chains are cross-linked by covalent bonds

questions.explanation: The planar rings keep the chains straight and the N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds between chains hold them in rigid sheets, giving great tensile strength.

questions.q: Which statement about disposing of polyalkenes is correct?

options.A: They can be hydrolysed back to their monomers
options.B: They can be recycled by melting and reshaping, or burned as fuel with controlled flue gas treatment
options.C: They biodegrade in landfill within a year

questions.explanation: Addition polymers are thermoplastics that can be remoulded, or incinerated to recover energy. Hydrolysis only works for condensation polymers.

questions.q: What is the general structure of an α-amino acid?
questions.explanation: In an α-amino acid the amine and carboxylic acid groups are attached to the same (α) carbon, which also carries an R group and a hydrogen.

questions.q: Which amino acid is NOT optically active?
questions.explanation: Glycine has two hydrogen atoms on the α-carbon, so it has no chiral centre. All other common amino acids are chiral.

questions.q: What is a zwitterion?

options.A: An ion with two positive charges
options.B: A molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge, with no overall charge

questions.explanation: At its isoelectric point an amino acid exists as H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻: the acid group has donated its proton to the amine group.

questions.q: What is the structure of alanine in a solution of low pH (strongly acidic)?
questions.explanation: In acid both groups are protonated: the amine becomes NH₃⁺ and the carboxylic acid stays as COOH, giving a positive ion.

questions.q: What is the structure of alanine in a solution of high pH (strongly alkaline)?
questions.explanation: In alkali the carboxylic acid loses its proton to COO⁻ and the amine group is unprotonated, giving a negative ion.

questions.q: Why do amino acids have relatively high melting points for their molecular size?

options.B: They exist as zwitterions, so strong ionic attractions act between them
options.D: They are gases at room temperature

questions.explanation: In the solid state amino acids are zwitterions, and the electrostatic attraction between opposite charges requires a lot of energy to overcome.

questions.q: Which bond links amino acids together in a protein?
questions.explanation: The COOH of one amino acid condenses with the NH₂ of the next to form a –CO–NH– peptide link with the loss of water.

questions.q: How many different dipeptides can be formed from two different amino acids, X and Y, using one of each?
questions.explanation: X–Y (X's acid group to Y's amine) and Y–X are different molecules, so two dipeptides are possible.

questions.q: Which describes the primary structure of a protein?

options.A: The sequence of amino acids in the chain

questions.explanation: Primary structure is the order of amino acids held by peptide bonds. Secondary is the local folding (helix or sheet), tertiary the overall 3D shape.

questions.q: Which interaction holds the α-helix in a protein's secondary structure?

options.B: Hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O groups of the peptide links

questions.explanation: The helix is held in shape by hydrogen bonds between the N–H of one peptide link and the C=O of another further along the chain.

questions.q: Which interaction forms between cysteine residues in the tertiary structure of a protein?
questions.explanation: Two cysteine side chains (CH₂SH) are oxidised to form a covalent S–S bridge, one of the strongest links holding the tertiary structure.

questions.q: How is a protein hydrolysed to its constituent amino acids in the laboratory?

options.A: Heating with concentrated hydrochloric acid under reflux

questions.explanation: Peptide bonds are hydrolysed by heating with 6 mol dm⁻³ HCl under reflux for several hours (or by enzymes in the body).

questions.q: In thin-layer chromatography of amino acids, why is the plate sprayed with a developing agent after running?

options.A: To fix the amino acids to the plate
options.B: Amino acids are colourless so a developing agent (ninhydrin) is needed to see them

questions.explanation: Ninhydrin reacts with amino acids to give purple spots, allowing the Rf values to be measured and compared with known values.

questions.q: What is the Rf value of a spot that travels 3.0 cm when the solvent front travels 7.5 cm?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by the spot / distance moved by the solvent front = 3.0 / 7.5 = 0.40.

questions.q: Which statement about enzymes is correct?

options.B: They are proteins whose active site binds a substrate with a specific shape, and they are stereospecific
options.D: They are used up in reactions

questions.explanation: The active site has a specific 3D shape that only the correct substrate (and often only one enantiomer) fits, like a lock and key.

questions.q: How do many drugs work on enzymes?

options.B: They have a shape similar to the substrate and block the active site (inhibition)
options.C: They are substrates that react faster

questions.explanation: Drug molecules designed to fit the active site act as inhibitors, preventing the natural substrate binding. Computers are used to model the fit.

questions.q: Which base pairs are found in DNA?

options.A: A with G, C with T
options.B: A with T, C with G
options.C: A with C, G with T
options.D: A with A, T with T

questions.explanation: Adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with thymine; cytosine forms three hydrogen bonds with guanine.

questions.q: How does cisplatin act as an anticancer drug?

options.A: It forms a coordinate bond between platinum and a nitrogen atom of guanine in DNA, preventing replication

questions.explanation: A chloride ligand on Pt is replaced by a nitrogen on a guanine base (ligand substitution), cross-linking the DNA strands so cancer cells cannot divide. It also damages healthy cells.

questions.q: Which sequence converts ethene into ethanoic acid?

options.A: Hydration to ethanol, then oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ under reflux

questions.explanation: Ethene + steam (H₃PO₄ catalyst) gives ethanol, a primary alcohol. Heating under reflux with excess acidified dichromate oxidises it through the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol to an aldehyde?

options.A: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), distilling the product as it forms
options.B: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heating under reflux

questions.explanation: Distilling off the aldehyde as soon as it forms prevents further oxidation to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Which two-step route converts bromoethane into propanoic acid?

options.A: KCN in ethanol, then acid hydrolysis of the nitrile

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution with cyanide gives propanenitrile (one extra carbon), which is hydrolysed with dilute acid to propanoic acid.

questions.q: Which route increases the carbon chain length by one?

options.A: Reaction of a halogenoalkane with KCN

questions.explanation: The cyanide ion adds a carbon atom. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an alkene into an alkane?
questions.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation adds H₂ across the C=C double bond.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions convert ethanol into ethene?
questions.explanation: Dehydration (elimination) of an alcohol uses concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ with heat, or passing the vapour over hot aluminium oxide.

questions.q: Which reagent converts propan-1-ol into 1-bromopropane?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bromide, generated in situ from KBr and concentrated H₂SO₄, substitutes the OH group for Br.

questions.q: Which is the best route from benzene to phenylamine?
questions.explanation: Benzene is nitrated with conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ to nitrobenzene, which is reduced with tin and concentrated HCl followed by NaOH to give phenylamine.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an acyl chloride into an ester?
questions.explanation: Alcohols react with acyl chlorides by nucleophilic addition–elimination to form esters and HCl.

questions.q: Which is a key principle of green chemistry in organic synthesis?

options.A: Using as many steps as possible
options.B: High atom economy, fewer steps, less hazardous solvents and renewable feedstocks
options.C: Using toxic solvents to speed up the reaction

questions.explanation: Industrial routes aim to minimise waste and energy use and avoid hazardous reagents. Fewer steps raise the overall yield.

questions.q: Which sequence converts propanone to 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid?

options.A: KCN/H⁺ to form the hydroxynitrile, then acid hydrolysis

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic addition of HCN gives (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN, and hydrolysis of the nitrile group gives the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: What is the overall yield of a three-step synthesis if each step has a yield of 80%?
questions.explanation: Yields multiply: 0.80 × 0.80 × 0.80 = 0.512, so about 51%.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a nitrile into a carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: Acid hydrolysis of a nitrile with dilute HCl under reflux gives the carboxylic acid and ammonium chloride.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid?

options.B: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux

questions.explanation: Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids by excess acidified dichromate under reflux (or by Tollens' or Fehling's reagents in the test-tube tests).

questions.q: Which reagent converts a ketone into a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: Reduction with sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) adds H⁻ then H⁺ to the C=O, giving a secondary alcohol.

questions.q: Which sequence converts 1-bromobutane into butan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: Aqueous hydroxide ions act as a nucleophile, substituting Br for OH. Ethanolic KOH would cause elimination to but-1-ene instead.

questions.q: Which reagent converts 1-bromobutane into but-1-ene?
questions.explanation: In ethanol the hydroxide ion acts as a base and removes a proton, eliminating HBr to form the alkene.

questions.q: Which reagents are needed to convert ethanoic acid into ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are converted to acyl chlorides using sulfur dichloride oxide (SOCl₂) or phosphorus(V) chloride.

questions.q: Which product forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with phenylamine?
questions.explanation: The amine nitrogen attacks the acyl chloride, forming an N-substituted amide (an acylation of the amine).

questions.q: A synthesis starts with ethene and ends with ethylamine. Which route is correct?
questions.explanation: Electrophilic addition of HBr gives bromoethane, which undergoes nucleophilic substitution with excess ammonia to give the primary amine.

questions.q: Why is reflux used when oxidising a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid?

options.B: To keep the volatile reactants and intermediate aldehyde in the flask so oxidation goes to completion

questions.explanation: Reflux condenses and returns vapours so the mixture can be heated for a long time without losing the aldehyde, allowing complete oxidation.

questions.q: Which nucleus is detected in carbon-13 NMR?
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 has no nuclear spin so cannot be observed. The ¹³C isotope (about 1.1% abundance) has spin and gives the NMR signal.

questions.q: What is the reference compound used in NMR spectroscopy?
questions.explanation: TMS, Si(CH₃)₄, is set as δ = 0. It gives a single sharp peak, is inert, volatile and its 12 equivalent protons give a strong signal.

questions.q: Why is CDCl₃ used as a solvent in ¹H NMR rather than CHCl₃?

options.B: Deuterium does not give a signal in the ¹H region, so the solvent does not swamp the spectrum
options.C: It has a higher boiling point

questions.explanation: Deuterium (²H) resonates at a very different frequency, so deuterated solvents give no peaks in the proton spectrum.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol?
questions.explanation: The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, giving one peak, and the CH(OH) carbon gives another.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: All three carbons are in different environments: CH₃, CH₂ and CH₂OH.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol?
questions.explanation: The CH₃, CH₂ and OH protons are in three different environments.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol, what is the splitting pattern of the CH₂ peak (ignoring the OH)?
questions.explanation: The CH₂ protons have three neighbouring protons on the adjacent CH₃, so by the n+1 rule the signal is a quartet.

questions.q: Which splitting pattern is seen for a proton with two equivalent neighbouring protons?
questions.explanation: n + 1 rule: two neighbours give 2 + 1 = 3 lines, a triplet with intensities 1:2:1.

questions.q: What does the area under a peak in a ¹H NMR spectrum (the integration) show?

options.B: The relative number of protons in that environment

questions.explanation: The integration trace or ratio gives the relative numbers of equivalent protons causing each signal.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹H NMR spectrum of propanone, and what is the splitting?
questions.explanation: All six protons are equivalent (two identical CH₃ groups) and have no neighbouring protons on an adjacent carbon, so there is one singlet.

questions.q: Which compound gives a ¹H NMR spectrum with a triplet and a quartet in the ratio 3:2?
questions.explanation: Chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, has a CH₃ triplet (split by two CH₂ protons) and a CH₂ quartet, in the ratio 3:2 with no other peaks. Ethanol and ethyl ethanoate have extra peaks.

questions.q: What causes spin–spin splitting in ¹H NMR?

options.A: The magnetic field of protons on adjacent carbon atoms

questions.explanation: Protons on neighbouring carbons can align with or against the external field, slightly changing the field felt by the proton being observed.

questions.q: A ¹H NMR peak at δ 9.5 to 10 ppm indicates
questions.explanation: Aldehyde protons appear far downfield at about δ 9.5 to 10.0. Carboxylic acid protons are even further, at δ 10 to 12.

questions.q: A ¹³C NMR peak at about δ 200 ppm indicates

options.B: a C=O carbon in an aldehyde or ketone
